doc.title: Chuck Israels interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 11, 2021

title: Three drummers with Bill Evans: Motian, Bunker and Arnie Wise
summary: Israels compares Paul Motian, Larry Bunker and Arnie Wise, and recounts how Wise replaced Bunker after Joe Chambers was passed over.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: I’m trying to recall if during the time you were with Bill Evans if there was a change in drummers. © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
How did — wow — how did that — did it affect the way you approached the music?

I don’t think so. The first drummer was Paul Motian, who did a good job. I wasn’t completely enamored of his playing but I liked it. You know I didn’t find it very — I didn’t find it very beautiful, just the way he hit the drums. His sound. He was a kind of a vertical drummer. But it was okay and I was glad to be in the band and I don’t think I was thinking critically about it, I just don’t remember being — I don’t remember thinking very much about it at all. It certainly didn’t stop us from playing. The music was happening and it was fun. Then Paul left, I think partly because he found my playing a little more conventional — I think. I don’t really know. I would have to have asked and I didn’t. But I know he said at one point that he didn’t like my playing that much. And then I brought Larry Bunker into the band. And Larry Bunker is one of a number of drummers that I’ve worked with that were absolutely superb musicians. Just superb. And not only intuitive but also educated. It was in many ways a better musician than I. [doorbell] who’s at the door? Margot will have to get it. And that was a joy for me. I loved playing with Larry. It was, on every level it was perfect in terms of dynamics and sound quality and texture and volume and interaction and swing and all the things you would want. I can’t say enough about it, good. It was really great. Then Larry left and, for personal reasons, to get back to California, his father-in-law had died and he had to get back to his wife. And we were looking for somebody and Bill auditioned a drummer I thought was, named Joe Chambers, and I thought this guy’s going to be good. But Bill thought he was not yet developed enough. I didn’t understand exactly what he meant by that. But I said why don’t you try the guy I grew up playing with, Arnie Wise. And Arnie’s approach to playing was — the sound quality was very much like Larry’s. A very pretty drum sound. You could sit next to either of them, right next to the drumset, and have the band on the other side and you could hear through the drumset you could hear all the music on the other side. Arnie had that quality and so did Larry. So that’s — and Arnie made less of a — he was more like glue gluing the bass and piano parts together. He wasn’t much of an instigator of things.
But he would take the duet and meld that beautifully.
I’m working on a book so I’m verbally oriented at the moment. And yet it never really, it doesn’t substitute for hearing the music.
